title: The Shabbat walk
hookLine: a slow walk with nowhere to get to
tomorrow: can Shabbat be kept with nobody else at the table?

cards: Step counts, pace charts, a ring on the screen that closes when you've moved enough. Walking has become a scoreboard, and every walk has a goal.
The Talmud has two teachings about walking on Shabbat, and they seem to point opposite ways. One says: slow down, your Sabbath walk shouldn't look like your weekday walk. The other says: run.
Both are in the Talmud, and both are still quoted. Here they are, each at its best.

teach.b: The first view starts in Isaiah, who says to honor the Sabbath by not going your own ways and not chasing your business.
The Talmud hears that in your feet: your walking on Shabbat should not be like your walking on a weekday. No rushing strides, no errands. A walk with nowhere to get to.
Its best case: hurry is how a weekday lives in the body. You can't rest while your legs are still racing to a meeting.
The second view comes from a sage, Rabbi Zeira. He says that when he first saw the sages running to hear a lesson on Shabbat, he thought they were breaking it.
Then he heard a teaching: a person should always run toward words of Torah, even on the Sabbath. So he ran too. Its best case: slowness was never the point; love is.
You hurry toward what you love, and Shabbat shouldn't make you hide that. The Talmud keeps both, side by side, and adds one more detail. Going to the synagogue, it's a mitzvah to run.
Leaving, don't take long strides, as if glad to get away.
Saba's stroll and a sprint to the synagogue door both keep the day; what differs is what the feet are for. So the Shabbat walk has a direction. Toward something you love, as quick as you like.
Everywhere else, slow, with nowhere to get to.

how: Some families take a slow walk on Shabbat afternoon, to a park or to visit friends, with no errands; walking to synagogue is part of the day for those who keep Shabbat by traditional law.

o: a walk to synagogue and then straight back home
a brisk walk to stay fit on the day of rest
a slow walk on the day of rest, with no errands

games.q: two ways to walk — tap the pairs.

s: the Talmud says your Sabbath walk shouldn't look like your weekday walk
Rabbi Zeira always thought running on Shabbat was fine
at first he thought the running sages were breaking it. then he heard a teaching, and ran too.
on Shabbat the tradition forbids hurrying for any reason
hurrying toward a mitzvah, like synagogue or a lesson, is welcomed.

games.q: your friend says the rule is simple: on Shabbat, always walk slowly. what's the best case for the other side?
o: Rabbi Zeira's: you run toward Torah, even on Shabbat, because you hurry toward what you love.
exercise matters, and the body needs a fast walk on a rest day too.
Isaiah tells people to hurry on the Sabbath, so slow walking came later.
games.why: both views are in the Talmud. slow down for your own business; run toward a mitzvah. a steelman keeps both.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly, inside or out, with nowhere to get to: a room, a hallway, a stretch of sidewalk. Let each step take a little longer than it wants to.
If walking isn't possible right now, rest your feet flat on the floor and feel their weight, one slow step at a time.

wordCard.voice: The Shabbat walk: slow toward nothing in particular, quick only toward something you love.

carryVoice: Keep this: nowhere to get to, unless it's toward something you love. Slow down, see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 113a (your walking on Shabbat should not be like your walking on a weekday)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 6b (Rabbi Zeira runs to the lesson on Shabbat; running to synagogue; no long strides when leaving)
